newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tumbling gold pulls back ground in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Tumbling gold pulls back ground in Asia.

text.p: Tumbling gold prices took a breather in Asia on Tuesday as short covering and bargain hunting in the Far East appeared to give a temporary respite to prices which have fallen to 3-1/4-year lows, dealers said.

The precious metal has shed $10 an ounce in the first week of 1997, battered by heavy selling from U.S. investment funds which have opted to switch their cash to booming stock and bond markets, leaving gold poised for further losses, they said.

At midday on Tuesday, spot gold was quoted in Hong Kong at US$358.30/$358.80 an ounce, slightly up from New York's overnight $357.50/$358 close and the lowest price fix since October 7, 1993 in London on Monday afternoon at $358.50.

"The shorts in the market seem to be the funds and they're pushing the market lower, and there's no investor interest to meet that sort of selling," said Dick Gazmararian, Hong Kong-based executive vice president of precious metals in the Asia Pacific for Republic National Bank.
"The funds remain enormously short and the market (could see) a further push on the downside," Gazmararian told Reuters.
The dollar's retreat from Monday's 45-month peak of 117 yen encouraged some Japanese arbitrage buying of spot gold on Tuesday. The U.S. currency was trading at 115.15 yen at midday in Tokyo.
Japanese trade houses were selling Tokyo gold futures in relatively firmer yen and buying spot gold in dollars.

"There is good buying out of Tokyo lending support. It'll probably hold around here. The market is probably looking to make a base around $357 if at all possible," said Jonathan Spall, head of precious metals in Asia for Deutsche Bank AG.

Japanese traders said the continuing soaring rally in U.S. stocks, despite the forecast of many analysts, a lack of inflation fears, the stronger dollar and concerns over central bank gold sales, all pointed to further heavy selling of gold.

These factors were more than outweighing solid Asian physical demand for gold as prices fell, particularly in India, and a short-term supply shortage in the distribution centres of Singapore and Hong Kong caused by Christmas refinery shutdowns. "Every factor suggests gold is heading south," said one dealer at a large Tokyo trading house. "Initial support at $350 (an ounce) would be the first target. Gold could test $350 after the options expiry on COMEX (New York) this coming Friday."
"Although the market is currently short, this is not a time to expect any lift from short covering. Rather, investment funds are putting on fresh short positions," he said.
Traders said the surprising rise in the U.S. stock market and a move to establish fresh market positions at the beginning of the New Year were combining to set a trend for gold.
"No floor is in sight at this stage and I think gold will test the downside for most of the first quarter of this year," a senior dealer at a foreign bank said.
The dealer said he would not rule out the possibility of gold tumbling to $330 if central bank sales actually took place.

One trader said that recent expressions of concern by Japanese over the yen's decline against the U.S. dollar could stimulate heavy long liquidation by individual investors on TOCOM (Tokyo commodities exchange), which could put additional pressure on the spot gold market.

"Private investors have been tending to hunt for bargains recently, backed by perceptions that the yen will fall further, but a possible change in the currency market could prompt investors to liquidate their longs," one Japanese analyst said.
Australian dealers said gold lease rates were ticking higher as some operators borrowed gold to sell and short the market.
"If they sell, they must borrow gold to fund their positions," said Mark Freemantle, senior gold trader for Rothschild Australia Ltd. "That's pushing the gold buying out again."
As a result, one-month gold lease rates are runnning at about 2.3 percent, with the 12-month rate at around 2.25 percent. A more typical rate is closer to 1.5 percent.
"It looked like it was easing until this last bout of selling, which caused a swing in the forwards again," Fremantle said.
Australian dealers expressed concern that a formidable technical marker at $360 an ounce failed to halt gold's decline, which has opened the gates for even steeper price falls.
The dealers would not rule out gold slipping to between $340 and $350 an ounce although most think these levels would attract fresh buying.
"Three-hundred and sixty (dollars) was supposed to be a significant support point and it traded through that like it almost didn't exist," one said.
"There's obviously good selling out there, and you've just got to go with the trend.
